title: ICICI Bank Doubles Overseas Borrowing Limit to $5 Billion as Indian Banks Race to Raise Dollars
excerpt: India's second-largest private lender has already raised $2.05 billion in dollar debt this month and is negotiating a $1.45 billion syndicated loan, as the RBI's concessional swap window nears its August 31 deadline.
body:
• ICICI Bank's board approved doubling its overseas borrowing limit to $5 billion, up from the previous $2.5 billion ceiling.
  • The bank has already raised $2.05 billion through dollar debt in the past month — the most among Indian banks since the RBI opened its concessional swap window in June.
  • Indian banks are racing to raise at least $5 billion collectively in dollar bonds and loans before the RBI closes its foreign-exchange swap facility on August 31, a month earlier than originally planned.
  • ICICI Bank is also in talks for a $1.45 billion syndicated dollar loan with Bank of America and other international lenders.

ICICI Bank said on Friday that its board approved doubling the limit for overseas borrowings to $5 billion, a move that positions India's second-largest private lender to significantly expand its international fundraising at a time when the window for cheap dollar hedging is narrowing.

The bank has already been the most active Indian issuer in dollar debt markets over the past month, raising $2.05 billion since the Reserve Bank of India announced a concessional foreign-exchange swap facility in early June, according to Reuters.

Why Banks Are Rushing to Raise Dollars

The urgency stems from the RBI's decision to bring forward the closure of its forex swap window to August 31 — a full month ahead of the original September 30 deadline. The facility allows banks and state-owned companies to hedge eligible external commercial borrowings at a fixed annual rate of 1.5%, well below prevailing market costs.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=eHWl48_SeZ4

That subsidy has made overseas fundraising unusually attractive. Private and state-run Indian lenders are collectively on track to raise at least $5 billion through a combination of bonds and loans in the next two weeks, four bankers told Reuters.

"We will have one of the busiest windows for the next 6-8 days from India. Few institutions who are not ready may need to drop their plan if it was solely meant for FCNR leverage."

— Akshay Naik, India head of debt capital markets, Citi

ICICI's Dollar Fundraising Blitz

ICICI Bank's $2.05 billion in dollar issuances over the past month represents its most aggressive international debt push in nearly a decade. The bank's first dollar bond sale in almost nine years came in July, when it raised $1 billion through a five-year paper at 100 basis points over U.S. Treasuries — well inside initial guidance of 130 basis points, with a 5.46% coupon.

It followed that with a $300 million reissuance at a yield of 5.352%, and then this week's $750 million five-year bond at 105 basis points over Treasuries, priced at a coupon of 5.417%. The latest offering drew bids worth over $2 billion, according to Reuters. All proceeds are designated for general corporate purposes, rated Baa3 by Moody's and BBB by S&P.

In addition to bond sales, ICICI Bank is negotiating a syndicated offshore loan of approximately $1.45 billion. Bank of America initially signed a $1 billion loan agreement, with the deal now being upsized to include Mizuho Bank, Mashreqbank, and United Overseas Bank, according to The Hindu Business Line. The four-year loan carries a margin of 110 basis points over the Secured Overnight Financing Rate.

A Broader Wave of Indian Dollar Debt

ICICI Bank's fundraising is part of a sector-wide trend. HDFC Bank became the first lender to tap the RBI's swap facility, raising $750 million through five-year bonds in June. Axis Bank followed with an $800 million dual-tranche dollar bond issue. State-run lenders including State Bank of India, Bank of Baroda, and Punjab National Bank are each targeting raises of $250 million to $500 million.

The rush reflects broader economic pressures. The RBI introduced the swap facility as part of a package to attract foreign-currency inflows and support the rupee, which has been under sustained pressure from the geopolitical fallout of the Iran crisis. By lowering hedging costs, the central bank incentivized banks to raise dollars overseas that can be lent domestically, supporting rupee liquidity and credit growth.

What Comes Next

With the August 31 deadline approaching, the pace of issuance is expected to intensify. Banks that have not yet completed their fundraising face the prospect of either accelerating their processes or abandoning plans altogether, particularly those designed solely to exploit the FCNR leverage opportunity.

For ICICI Bank, the expanded $5 billion borrowing ceiling provides significant headroom. With $2.05 billion already raised in bonds and a potential $1.45 billion loan in the pipeline, the bank has utilized roughly $3.5 billion of its new limit, leaving room for additional issuances if market conditions remain favorable before the swap window shuts.
